This is a game, not therapy. If someone controls or scares you, talk to someone you trust or a helpline.
Story and advice: John Gray, Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus (1992). The book says men and women are very different. Studies find we're alike in most ways. The coloured lights show what research says. Reader data: {reviews} reviews and {quotes} Goodreads quotes, read {date}.

how.title: How I built it · Swipe the Moment
how.lede: A 30-second game that turns a 1992 relationship book into choices you can practise. Every idea is checked twice: what readers love, and what research says.
how.s1.title: Ask the readers
how.s1.p1: I read {reviews} reviews on Goodreads, StoryGraph, Google Play and Amazon. I also matched {quotes} popular quotes to the chapter they come from.
how.s1.p2: My first guesses about the quotes were wrong 21 times out of 43, so I checked each one against the book's text.
how.s2.title: Check the research
how.s2.p1: Each idea got a coloured light. Green means research backs it, amber means it partly does, red means research disagrees, and grey means I found no study that tests it.
how.s2.p2: Only one idea is both loved by readers and backed by research: feeling needed and cherished.
how.s3.title: Map the ideas
how.s3.p1: I drew how the 13 ideas lead into each other, with one small daily action for each.
how.s3.alt: The idea map: 13 ideas, each with a reader rank, a research light and a daily action
how.s3.cap: The idea map, drawn in Excalidraw.
how.s4.title: Sketch, then cut the words
how.s4.p1: My first sketches had too many words. So I planned the first 30 seconds, second by second: you play first and choose later.
how.s4.alt1: An early text-heavy wireframe of a scenario game
how.s4.alt2: The Swipe the Moment storyboard, from 0 to 30 seconds
how.s4.cap2: After: a 30-second storyboard with almost no words.
how.s5.title: Pick the look
how.s5.p1: At first I made the two planets neutral. Then I matched the book: Mars is the men and Venus is the women. The research lights stay, so you always see both sides.
how.s5.alt: Early cast sheet with two planet characters and the objects for each idea
how.s5.cap: The early cast sheet. Each idea became one object: a cave, a wave, a plant, a heat meter.
how.s6.title: Build it with two AI partners
how.s6.p1: I worked with Claude Code, running Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. It did the research runs, drew the sketches, wrote the game in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and tested it.
how.s6.p2: I used Codex, running OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol, for two jobs: it translated every word of the game into Vietnamese, and it reviewed the code and the translation before launch. Claude Code then fixed what Codex found.
how.s6.p3: The game's words live in two text files, one for English and one for Vietnamese. Another file joins the moments with the research. Before each build, a check stops if a habit has no source link or if the two languages don't match. Your progress stays in the page while you play; nothing is saved, and the link is shared only if you tap Share.
how.s7.title: Test it
how.s7.p1: I played both planets, in both languages, in a phone-size browser. Two new readers also checked the English words, and their ease score rose from 2 to 3 out of 5.
how.s7.alt: The finished game: a swipe card with two round buttons
how.h1: The "good" replies are my reading of the book. The research lights cover each idea, not each reply.
how.h2: Few reviews name one idea; most talk about the whole book.
how.h3: I tested in a phone-size browser, not on every phone. A native Vietnamese speaker has not checked the translation yet.
how.h4: This is a game, not therapy.
